In mathematics, and particularly [[general topology]], the '''half-disk topology''' is an example of a [[topology]] given to the set <Math>X</Math>, given by all points <Math>(x,y)</Math> in the plane such that <Math>y\ge 0</Math>.<ref name="CEIT1">{{Citation|first1=L. A.|last1=Steen|first2=J. A.|last2=Seebach|title=[[Counterexamples in Topology]]|publisher=Dover|year=1995|pages=96–97|isbn=0-486-68735-X}}</ref> The set <Math>X</Math> can be termed the closed upper half plane.

== Construction == 

We consider <Math>X</Math> to consist of the open upper half plane <Math>P</Math>, given by all points <Math>(x,y)</Math> in the plane such that <Math>y>0</Math>; and the ''x''-axis <Math>L</Math>, given by all points <Math>(x,y)</Math> in the plane such that <Math>y=0</Math>. Clearly <Math>X</Math> is given by the [[union (set theory)|union]] <Math>P\cup L</Math>. The open upper half plane <Math>P</Math> has a topology given by the [[Euclidean space|Euclidean]] [[Metric_topology#Open_and_closed_sets.2C_topology_and_convergence|metric topology]].<ref name="CEIT1"/> We extend the topology on <Math>P</Math> to a topology on <Math>X=P\cup L</Math> by adding some additional open sets. These extra sets are of the form <Math>{(x,0)}\cup (P\cap U)</Math>, where <Math>(x,0)</Math> is a point on the line <Math>L</Math> and <Math>U</Math> is a [[neighbourhood (topology)|neighbourhood]] of <Math>(x,0)</Math> in the plane, open with respect to the [[Euclidean metric]] (defining the disk radius).<ref name="CEIT1"/>

== Properties of <math>X</math> ==

This topology results in a space satisfying the following properties.

* <math>X</math> is [[Hausdorff Space|Hausdorff]] (and thus also <math>T_0</math> and <math>T_1</math>).

* <math>X</math> is not [[Regular space|regular]] and therefore not [[Normal space|normal]].

* <math>L</math> with the [[Subspace topology|subspace topology]] of <math>X</math> is [[Discrete space|discrete]], so <math>X</math> is not [[Second-countable space|second-countable]].

* <math>X</math> is [[Separable space|separable]]. A countably dense subset is given by the rational points <math>X\cap\mathbb{Q}</math>.
